'''Paul K. Hansma''' (born April 28, 1946) is an American [[physicist]] at the [[University of California, Santa Barbara]].<ref>{{Cite web | url=http://hansmalab.physics.ucsb.edu/ |title = Hansma Research Group – Department of Physics, UC Santa Barbara}}</ref>

==Early life and education==
Paul K. Hansma was born in Salt Lake City, Utah.<ref>{{Cite web | url=https://oh.sciencehistory.org/oral-histories/hansma-paul-k |title = Paul K. Hansma &#124; Science History Institute &#124; Center for Oral History}}</ref> He received his undergraduate degree from [[New College of Florida]], and his PhD in physics from the [[University of California, Berkeley]] where he studied electron tunneling and [[Josephson junctions]].<ref  name=APS>{{Cite web | url=https://www.aps.org/units/dbp/awards/recipient.cfm?first_nm=Paul&last_nm=Hansma&year=2000 |title = Recipient}}</ref>

==Career==
Hansma became an assistant professor at the [[University of California, Santa Barbara]] in 1974. He then became an associate professor three years later.<ref>{{Cite book | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=KjeOAwAAQBAJ&pg=PA153 | title=Public Universities and Regional Growth: Insights from the University of California| isbn=9780804791427| last1=Kenney| first1=Martin| last2=Mowery| first2=David C.| date=2014-06-18}}</ref> In the 1970s, Hansma began working in electron tunneling spectroscopy, and moved to STM-based experiments by the early 1980s.<ref>{{Cite book | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=0z5awb7w-X8C&pg=PA90 |title = Toward a Minor Architecture|isbn = 9780262300285|last1 = Stoner|first1 = Jill|date = 2012-03-09}}</ref> This included biological STM as of 1985, when he adapted his STM microscopes to work in water (previously STMs would only work in air).<ref>{{Cite book | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=0z5awb7w-X8C&pg=PA99 |title = Toward a Minor Architecture|isbn = 9780262300285|last1 = Stoner|first1 = Jill|date = 2012-03-09}}</ref>

Over the 1980s, Hansma worked in conjunction with [[IBM]] Zurich, researching the use of probe microscopy and its use in a variety of different fields.<ref>{{Cite book | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=0z5awb7w-X8C&pg=PA88 |title = Toward a Minor Architecture|isbn = 9780262300285|last1 = Stoner|first1 = Jill|date = 2012-03-09}}</ref> As a part of this work, he co-developed three scanning tunneling microscopes for the University of California, Santa Barbara.<ref>{{Cite book | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=GoWDDwAAQBAJ&pg=PA155 | title=Nanotech and the Humanities: An Anthropologist Observes the Science of Atoms and Molecules| isbn=9781527524255| last1=Toumey| first1=Chris P.| date=2019-01-07}}</ref> In the late 1980s,<ref>{{Cite web | url=https://www.newscientist.com/article/mg12216624-700-science-microscope-reveals-molecules-at-work/ |title = Science: Microscope reveals molecules at work}}</ref> Hansma then worked on the development of atomic force microscopes and their use in research.<ref>{{Cite book | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=tZ2r48U8V-MC&pg=PR13 |title = Atomic Force Microscopy in Cell Biology|isbn = 9780080549446|date = 2002-05-30}}</ref> This included the use of AFMs in genetic research, using them to observe DNA and RNA molecules in manner that did not disturb their natural interactions during the late 1990s.<ref>{{Cite web | url=https://www.science.org/content/article/dna-cliffhanger |title = DNA Cliffhanger|date = 1997-03-19}}</ref>

In 1991, Hansma researched the process of corrosion in infrastructure and other places like car batteries, and looked at the role the type of electrolyte involved has on the corrosion’s progress.<ref>{{Cite web | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=zAIugfGhlj8C&pg=RA1-PA20 | title=Popular Science| publisher=Bonnier Corporation| date=May 1991}}</ref> In 2005 Hansma’s discovered the existence of a [[biopolymer]] in human bones that provides a “glue” like function, correlatively strengthening or weakening the bone.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://pubs.acs.org/cen/news/83/i30/8330notw6.html|title = C&EN: Latest News - Biopolymer Gives Strength to Bones}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=6jG6KiqkVM8C&pg=PA14 |title = Findings, March 2006}}</ref> Around this time he also began to develop high-speed scanning AFMs.<ref>{{Cite book | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=AeFi6_rMoq4C&pg=PA112 | title=Roadmap of Scanning Probe Microscopy| isbn=9783540343158| last1=Morita| first1=Seizo| date=2006-12-30| bibcode=2006rspm.book.....M}}</ref> During his research into bone glue, Hansma developed the OsteoProbe,<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Diez-Perez |first1=A. |last2=Bouxsein |first2=M.L. |last3=Eriksen |first3=E.F. |last4=Khosla |first4=S. |last5=Nyman |first5=J.S. |last6=Papapoulos |first6=S. |last7=Tang |first7=S.Y. |title=Technical note: Recommendations for a standard procedure to assess cortical bone at the tissue-level in vivo using impact microindentation |journal=Bone Reports |date=December 2016 |volume=5 |pages=181–185 |doi=10.1016/j.bonr.2016.07.004 |pmid=27975078 |pmc=5152622 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web | url=https://www.keyt.com/news/santa-barbara-county/measuring-bone-strength-at-university-of-california-santa-barbara-/64751103 |title = Measuring Bone Strength at University of California Santa Barbara|date = 2014-09-18}}</ref> and also spent time researching the use of natural adhesives to create optimized adhesives for other applications.<ref>{{Cite web | url=https://phys.org/news/2007-01-natures-frugal-insight-optimized-adhesives.html |title = Nature's frugal glues provide insight for optimized adhesives}}</ref> He is also the developer of Reference Point Indentation, which tests bone quality.<ref>{{Cite web | url=https://www.noozhawk.com/article/bizhawk_downtown_medicine_shoppe_pharmacy_shutters_doors_20131211 |title = BizHawk: Medicine Shoppe Pharmacy Closes After Two Decades Downtown| date=12 December 2013 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web | url=https://www.independent.com/news/2010/aug/09/ucsb-prof-validates-new-bone-quality-testing-tool/ |title = UCSB Prof Validates New Bone-Quality Testing Tool|date = 2010-08-09}}</ref> He is also the inventor of Scanning Ion Conductance Microscopy.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Kim |first1=Joonhui |last2=Kim |first2=Seong-Oh |last3=Cho |first3=Nam-Joon |title=Alternative configuration scheme for signal amplification with scanning ion conductance microscopy |journal=Review of Scientific Instruments |date=February 2015 |volume=86 |issue=2 |pages=023706 |doi=10.1063/1.4907360 |pmid=25725851 |bibcode=2015RScI...86b3706K |doi-access=free |hdl=10356/107021 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>

==Recognition==
Hansma is the namesake of the Paul Hansma Research Group at the Department of Physics of the University of California, Santa Barbara.<ref>{{Cite web | url=https://www.laboratoryequipment.com/article/2013/06/technology-spurs-expansion-afm-scanning-range |title = Technology Spurs Expansion of AFM Scanning Range|date = 2013-06-27}}</ref> In 1964 he was named a Presidential Scholar by President Lyndon Johnson.<ref>{{Cite web | url=https://newspaperarchive.com/scottsdale-progress-jun-03-1964-p-1/ |title = Scottsdale Progress Newspaper Archives, Jun 3, 1964|date = 1964-06-03}}</ref> He is a fellow of the [[American Physical Society]] and the American Association for the Advancement of Science, and was the 2000 recipient of the Max Delbruck Prize in Biological Physics.<ref name=APS />
